cells.tense: Right now your eye is landing clean on the work and your hands are keeping pace.
cells.act: read the hardest page of it twice, slowly, before you stop
cells.ask: On some day soon, take the hardest stretch of the work and go through it twice, slow, starting again from the top before you put anything down.
cells.core:
In that small spot where you do the same thing over until it goes smooth, a first clean look is available to you — you see what you are working on before you have sorted it into anything. Nothing has been decided yet, and that is the part worth keeping. The thing stays open long enough to be seen properly, and repetition has been quietly building exactly this.

There is nothing to add to how you work. Give the deepest part a second pass instead — the stretch you would normally skim because it stopped being new. Begin there, stay with it until a detail you had been walking past shows itself, then set the work down. The equal measure is the point. Your eye will cut into things soon enough; today it only has to rest on them.
cells.sheetLine: You can look at a thing before you name it.
cells.verb: catching the first clean look at something before you name it
cells.place: the small quiet spot where you do the same thing over until it goes smooth

cells.tense: Soon enough the seeing will not feel like enough, and you will be shoving the next stage forward before it gets here.
cells.act: let what was only possible stand finished
cells.ask: When a piece of work is done, walk away and change nothing, add nothing, and stop deciding what it is for.
cells.core:
You keep sharpening how you see something and you want the next version of it settled before it has actually shown up. So the hours that would go into looking go into arranging — doors opened early, the next shape sketched before this one has finished, a step laid down before it has grown under you. From in there, that registers as being ready. From out here, nothing gets to arrive at its own pace.

A finished thing can be left where it stands. Take one piece of work all the way to its end, then keep your hands off whatever it suggests next. Adding nothing is not standing still. The space you keep guarding against is already here, and it will keep.

cells.tense: For a long while your eye has not been arriving at the work, though the work keeps getting done.
cells.act: complete the form so it stands without you
cells.ask: Carry some half-finished piece all the way to done, then set it where you will see it standing finished.
cells.core:
The thing you do over and again still gets done, and you are not in it while it happens. Old rhythm carries what used to be fresh attention — the same motions in the same order, nothing new coming through them, and you put each one down before it is complete. What was meant to sharpen how you see is running with nothing sharp in it.

Rather than trying to be more present, close something all the way. Take a half-finished piece and carry it to the end — not tidy, finished — then set it somewhere your eye will fall on it. That keeps your hands busy while your attention comes back through them. Attention does come back, and it comes back through something completed rather than something feared.
cells.sheetLine: The motions keep going and your eye does not.

cells.tense: You are already catching what is new in the work while telling yourself it is just how it goes.
cells.act: meet what is arriving as it arrives
cells.ask: In the middle of a session, notice one shift in what your hands are doing before you name it, and hold it a moment instead of filing it under habit.
cells.core:
Midway through the doing, something is being caught — a change in what your hands are actually up to, a part that has loosened since the last time — and it goes under habit. Nothing about what you notice is claimed, so it reads as the work running by itself, old as the routine. The fresh part gets filed with the rest and the routine gets the credit for it.

That first look belongs to you. In a session, catch what you notice before you have a label for it, and hold it the length of one breath. Something else will come after; your attention keeps arriving whether or not anyone signs for it, and signing for it is only the work catching up to where you already are.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person keeps a practice going at all — the draw says perception is dawning in Discipline, not that a routine exists; a reader could say nothing in their week is sitting in a seat of repetition, and the ask would still hold because a single slow look in anything done by hand is available on any day. The sentence that serves me more than them is 'the practice is the point' — the draw is about seeing, and the seat is only where the seeing lands; the reach is if I say where their looking went, since the record says clarity is unspent, not that they looked away.
